newsitem.title: UK: Film director Zinnemann dies of heart attack.
newsitem.headline: Film director Zinnemann dies of heart attack.

text.p: Film director Fred Zinnemann, the maker of "High Noon," and "From Here to Eternity" has died in London of a heart attack, his son said on Saturday.
Tim Zinnemann, a film producer, told reporters the death on Friday came as a shock to the family who had been planning celebrations for his father's 90th birthday on April 29.

Austrian-born Zinnemann won Oscars for the 1953 film "From Here to Eternity" and the 1966 film "A Man for All Seasons", as well as acclaim for classics such as "The Day of The Jackal," "Julia" and "The Nun's Story".
Zinnemann said his father would have made a perfect character in one of his classic films.
"He was like the characters in those wonderful movies such as All Quiet On The Western Front' or From Here To Eternity'. He always showed courage, honour and fortitude.
"He always stuck to his guns no matter what, whether the cause was popular or not. He was a maverick in the Hollywood system, able to make any kind of film," Tim Zinnemann said.
Zinnemann said his father, who moved to London more than 30 years ago, kept his two Oscars hidden away..
"My father was a very modest man. He kept them locked in a cabinet with instructions that they should not go on display," he said.
He said the family was planning a memorial service in Los Angeles on April 29, which would have been his father's 90th birthday.
During his 40-year career Zinnemann made about 20 films and worked with such top stars as Gary Cooper and Audrey Hepburn. He introduced Marlon Brando to filmgoers in "The Men" in 1950.

He largely stopped making films after "Five Days One Summer" with Sean Connery in 1982 partly because of age and health problems and partly because he was dispirited by the vicious reviews the film received.
Born in Vienna, Zinnemann started out to become a violinist but abandoned a career in music when he decided he had no talent. He next studied law, earning a degree at the University of Vienna.

But he was impressed by film while a student and in 1927 went to Paris as one of the first students of the Ecole Tehnique de Cinema, where he started by learning optics, photochemistry, development and printing, and worked as an assistant camerman.

He first tackled Hollywood in 1929 as an extra in "All Quiet on the Western Front." He worked his way up from film cutter to an assistant to directors Berthold Viertol, Robert Flaherty and Busby Berkeley.
